note: A reading, not the text's statement. FOR: the same name; the same time -- Salmon, the father of Boaz by Rahab (Matt 1:5), is the son of Nahshon (Ruth 4:20), who led Judah in the wilderness (Num 1:7), and Rahab of Jericho 'has lived among the Israelites to this day' (Josh 6:25); Matthew names four women in the line besides Mary, and three of them (Tamar 1:3, Ruth 1:5, Uriah's wife 1:6) have their story told elsewhere; and Matthew shortens lines elsewhere (Joram is 'the father of Uzziah', Matt 1:8, while 1 Chr 3:11-12 lists Ahaziah, Joash and Amaziah between Joram and Azariah), so the short line from Salmon to David (Ruth 4:20-22; Matt 1:4-6) proves little either way. AGAINST: no verse joins them; Matthew says nothing of Jericho, and Joshua nothing of a marriage or a son (Josh 6:25); and the Greek spells the names differently -- Ῥαχάβ in Matt 1:5, Ῥαάβ in Heb 11:31 and Jas 2:25 -- though the difference may be only one of spelling. (Worded after the eight-reader review, 2026-10-03.)

A reading, not the text's statement. FOR: the lists of David's sons born in Jerusalem run in the same order -- 'Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon' (2Sam 5:14; 1Chr 14:4) and 'Shimea, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon' (1Chr 3:5) -- so Shimea stands where Shammua stands, with the same three names after him. AGAINST: no verse says Shimea and Shammua are one son; the two names are spelled differently; and the text does not lay the lists side by side, so the likeness of order is the whole of the case.

A reading, not the text's statement. FOR: Jesse's sons are listed 'The firstborn was Eliab, the second was Abinadab, and the third was Shammah' (1Sam 17:13) and 'Eliab his firstborn; Abinadab was born second, Shimea third' (1Chr 2:13) -- the same first two names, and the same third place. AGAINST: no verse says Shammah and Shimea are one man; the two names are spelled differently; and the lists do not agree on everything -- Samuel says Jesse 'had eight sons' (1Sam 17:12) while Chronicles names seven (1Chr 2:13-15) -- so the text does not present them as copies of one list.

A reading, not the text's statement. FOR: Shimeah is 'David's brother' (2Sam 13:3; a 'David's brother Shimei' is also named at 1Chr 20:7), and Shammah is the third of Jesse's sons (1Sam 17:13), which makes him David's brother too. AGAINST: no verse calls Shammah Shimeah, or names Shammah as the father of Jonadab or of Jonathan; the text names more than one brother of David (1Sam 17:13; 1Chr 2:13-15), so a brother named Shimeah need not be the one the Samuel list calls Shammah; and the names are spelled differently. (Worded after the eleven-reader review, 2026-10-13.)

A reading, not the text's statement. FOR: both are David's brother, and in Chronicles the Hebrew spells the two names alike -- 'Shimea third' among Jesse's sons (1Chr 2:13) and 'Jonathan the son of David's brother Shimei' (1Chr 20:7) are the same Hebrew word, though the Berean English gives Shimea in one place and Shimei in the other; Samuel's spelling of the name of a brother of David is Shimeah (2Sam 13:3). AGAINST: no verse says the Shimea of 1Chr 2:13 is the Shimeah of 2Sam 13:3, or that either is the father of Jonathan; Jonadab (2Sam 13:3) and Jonathan (1Chr 20:7) are named as different sons; and the Hebrew of Samuel ends differently (Shimeah, שִׁמְעָה) from the Hebrew of Chronicles (Shimea, שִׁמְעָא), though the difference may be only one of spelling. (Worded after the eleven-reader review, 2026-10-13.)

A reading, not the text's statement. FOR: Joktan's sons stand in the same order in Gen 10:28 and in 1Chr 1:22, and the Berean text reads the same words in both: 'Obal, Abimael, Sheba'. AGAINST: no verse says the two are one man; the Hebrew spells them differently -- Obal (עוֹבָל) in Gen 10:28 and Ebal (עֵיבָל) in 1Chr 1:22, which is why the graph holds two records, even though the Berean English gives 'Obal' at both -- and the difference may be only one of spelling; the name Ebal is also borne by a son of Shobal (Gen 36:23), so the spelling alone does not settle which man is meant.

A reading, not the text's statement. FOR: the two lists of Esau's wives each name a daughter of Elon the Hittite -- 'Basemath daughter of Elon the Hittite' (Gen 26:34) and 'Adah daughter of Elon the Hittite' (Gen 36:2). AGAINST: no verse says the two names are one woman; the names are different; Gen 36:3 also attaches the name Basemath to a woman described as 'Basemath daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebaioth', and Gen 36:10 names Adah as the mother of Eliphaz and Basemath as the mother of Reuel; and the lists differ in other names too (Judith daughter of Beeri in Gen 26:34, Oholibamah daughter of Anah in Gen 36:2). The text gives its lists of Esau's wives in different places and does not reconcile them, so the graph keeps both records; this is a tension the text holds, not something this link resolves. (Worded after the eleven-reader review, 2026-10-13.)

A reading, not the text's statement. FOR: Gen 28:9 names the wife Esau married as 'Mahalath, the sister of Nebaioth and daughter of Abraham's son Ishmael', and Gen 36:3 names 'Basemath daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebaioth' -- the same father and the same brother are named in each, with a different name for the daughter. AGAINST: no verse says the two names are one woman; the names are different; Mahalath is not named in Gen 36; and Basemath is also the name of a daughter of Elon the Hittite (Gen 26:34), so the name does not point to one woman alone. The text gives its lists of Esau's wives in different places and does not reconcile them, so the graph keeps both records; this is a tension the text holds, not something this link resolves. (Worded after the eleven-reader review, 2026-10-13.)

A reading, not the text's statement. FOR: the three Gospels tell one call in the same steps -- a man 'sitting at the tax booth', 'Follow Me', and he 'got up' and followed Him (Matt 9:9; Mark 2:14; Luke 5:27-28, where Luke adds that he 'left everything') -- and name him Matthew in Matt 9:9 and Levi in Mark 2:14 and Luke 5:27-28; in each a meal with many tax collectors follows (Matt 9:10; Mark 2:15; Luke 5:29), which Luke says was at Levi's house, while the Greek of Matt 9:10 says only 'the house'; Matthew's list of the Twelve calls him 'Matthew the tax collector' (Matt 10:3); and one man bearing two names is not strange, as in 'Simon, whom He named Peter' (Luke 6:14). AGAINST: no verse says Levi is Matthew; none of the three lists of the Twelve names Levi, and Mark and Luke list 'Matthew' without a second name (Mark 3:18; Luke 6:15), though Luke notes the second name where Simon has one (Luke 6:14); and 'son of Alphaeus' is said of Levi at Mark 2:14 and of James in the lists (Matt 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:15), so if Levi is Matthew then Matthew and James were sons of one Alphaeus, which no verse says, though two men may share the name. (Worded after the eleven-reader review, 2026-10-13.)
